lessons.title: Regular polygons and symmetry
lessons.summary: Use equal sides and corners to identify regular polygons and describe their symmetries.
lessons.objective: Use equal sides and corners to identify regular polygons and describe their symmetries.
lessons.before: A polygon is closed and has straight sides. For a regular polygon all side lengths and all corner sizes match.
lessons.ideas:
Count sides and check angles. A four-sided regular polygon is a square.

A non-square rectangle has two lines of symmetry through opposite side midpoints.

The order of rotational symmetry is the number of matches in 360°. An order of 1 means only the full turn matches.
lessons.method:
Explain both conditions when describing a regular shape.

Use a quick sketch and draw each mirror line fully.

For repeats of equal size, divide 360° by the order to find the smallest matching turn.
mistakes: Equal sides alone are not enough. A rhombus can have different corner angles.
A diagonal of a non-square rectangle does not reflect the whole shape onto itself.
Do not count the start and finish as two separate matches.

examples.title: A fence made to a regular shape
examples.question:
A regular polygon has 6 sides. Every side is 5 m long.

  1. How many lines of symmetry does the polygon have?

    [2]

  2. Find the perimeter.

    [2]

  3. Sketch an example and describe what makes it regular.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The shape is a regular hexagon.

It has the same number of mirror lines as sides, so there are 6.

\(6\).

(b) Add 6 lengths of 5 m.

\(30\) m.

(c) Mark equal sides with matching ticks. Check that each corner is the same size.

Sketch a regular hexagon. It has 6 equal sides and 6 equal angles.

examples.title: Mirror lines of a rectangle
examples.question:

  1. How many lines of symmetry does the sign have?

    [2]

  2. Explain whether the number of mirror lines changes if the two lengths become equal.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) One mirror line joins the midpoints of the two short sides.

The other joins the midpoints of the two long sides.

\(2\).

(b) With equal adjacent sides, each diagonal also reflects the shape onto itself.

It increases from 2 to 4. A square has the two midpoint lines and two diagonal lines.

examples.title: A rotating logo
examples.question:
A logo has 1 concentric rings. On each ring, the same pattern repeats in 4 identical equal sectors.

  1. What is its order of rotation?

    [2]

  2. How many degrees is its smallest non-zero matching turn?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The full turn is split into 4 equal matching steps.

The starting orientation at the completed turn counts once.

\(4\).

(b) Divide \(360^\circ\) by 4.

\(90\) degrees.

lessons.title: Matching shapes, circles and drawing lines
lessons.summary: Match corresponding parts, name circle features and draw parallel or perpendicular sides.
lessons.objective: Match corresponding parts, name circle features and draw parallel or perpendicular sides.
lessons.before: Congruent shapes have the same shape and size. Turning or reflecting one does not change the side lengths.
lessons.ideas:
Use the named correspondence to match corners and sides. The order of letters matters.

A chord joins two points on the circumference. A diameter is a chord through the centre. A tangent touches at exactly one point.

Parallel lines have a constant gap and never cross. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°. Use the right-angled corner of the set square for a perpendicular edge.
lessons.method:
Mark equal sides with matching ticks and give equal angles matching arcs.

Mark the centre before identifying a diameter.

Use a small right-angle square to mark perpendicular sides.
mistakes: Matching the longest-looking side can be misleading when a diagram is not to scale.
Radius and diameter are distances across part or all of the circle. Circumference refers to the boundary.
Edges pointing in different directions cannot be parallel, even if they have the same length.

\(7\) cm.

(b) Match B with Q and C with R.

\(2\) cm.

(c) C is the middle letter because the angle is at C. Match each letter in order.

Angle QRP.

    [2]

  3. What is a straight line that touches the circle at just one point called?

\(19\) mm.

(b) Both endpoints are on the circumference.

(c) The touch point is on the circumference.

A tangent.

lessons.title: Area units, triangles and compound shapes
lessons.summary: Convert square units, explain the triangle formula and find the area of a composite shape.
lessons.objective: Convert square units, explain the triangle formula and find the area of a composite shape.
lessons.before: A square centimetre is 10 mm long and 10 mm wide. There are 100 square millimetres inside it.
lessons.ideas:
Use the length conversion in both directions across the square. Also, one hectare is 10,000 square metres.

The area is \(\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{perpendicular height}\). Use the height at 90° to the base.

Find the areas separately, then add shapes that do not overlap. Subtract a cut-out from a larger shape if that is easier.
lessons.method:
Write the conversion with squared units, then check the direction.

Mark the right angle and label the height before working out the area.

Label any missing dimensions you can deduce before finding areas.
mistakes: One centimetre is 10 mm, but one square centimetre is 100 square millimetres.
A sloping side is not usually the perpendicular height.
Shared edges are not extra regions. Count each inside area once.

examples.title: Converting a measured area
examples.question:
A parcel map records a region with area 1500 mm². There are 2 regions of that size.

  1. Convert the area of one region to cm².

    [2]

  2. Find the total area of all 2 regions, in cm².

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) One cm² equals 100 mm².

Divide 1500 by 100.

\(15\) cm².

(b) Each region takes 15 cm².

\(30\) cm².

(b) Turn one copy over a shared edge or use the matching enclosing rectangle.

lessons.title: Solid shapes and volume
lessons.summary: Identify three-dimensional solids and find volume by counting layers or adding cuboids.
lessons.objective: Identify three-dimensional solids and find volume by counting layers or adding cuboids.
lessons.before: Describe both flat and curved surfaces. An edge is where faces or surfaces meet. A vertex is a corner.
lessons.ideas:
A prism has matching polygonal ends and a fixed cross-section. A pyramid has one base and triangular faces meeting at a point.

A cylinder has two circular ends. A cone has one circular base and one vertex. A sphere has no flat faces.

Volume of a cuboid is length × width × height, in cubic units.

Find each volume using the three dimensions of that cuboid. Add them together.
lessons.method:
Name the end shape to describe a prism precisely.

Choose a precise name and support it with more than one property.

Write cubic units after the answer.

Label dimensions for each part before multiplying.
mistakes: Count each vertex once, even when it belongs to several faces.
A circular base is a flat face. A curved side does not make the base curved.
Area counts squares. Volume counts cubes.
The length along the whole solid may be different from the length of one part.

examples.title: A display of prisms
examples.question:
A display has 2 identical hexagonal prisms. Each has a 6-sided polygon at each end.

  1. How many faces does one prism have?

    [2]

  2. How many vertices does one prism have?

    [2]

  3. Find the total number of faces, counting each prism separately.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are two end faces.

There are 6 side faces, one for each edge of the end face.

\(8\).

(b) There are 6 vertices on each end.

\(12\).

(c) Each of the 2 prisms has 8 faces.

\(16\).

(b) Look at the presence or lack of a flat face.

examples.solution:
(a) The first base has area 22 m².

Multiply by the height 3 m to get 66 m³.

Draw the outline that an observer sees from the stated direction. Equal features must align between views.

Use matching heights between a front view and a side view. The horizontal dimension changes.

lessons.title: Angles around points and on lines
lessons.summary: Find unknown angles and explain each step using angle facts.
lessons.objective: Find unknown angles and explain each step using angle facts.
lessons.before: Imagine a full turn around the corner of a page. Wherever you start, the complete turn is 360°.
lessons.ideas:
When neighbouring angles exactly fill the turn, add known angles and subtract from 360°.

Each triangle has angle sum 180°. The two sums give 360° for the quadrilateral.

Corresponding and alternate angles are equal. Co-interior angles add to 180°. Vertically opposite angles at one crossing are equal.

Use 90° as the total when the question states that the lines are perpendicular or shows a right-angle mark.
lessons.method:
Name the angle fact you use before doing the subtraction.

If a diagram is misleading, use the stated sizes and the angle fact.

Write the angle fact next to each step.

Check which total fits the angle fact, 90°, 180° or 360°.
mistakes: A straight line is half a turn, 180°. Around a point is a full turn.
The quadrilateral need not be a rectangle for the sum to hold.
The parallel-line rules need the two lines to be parallel. A right angle needs lines that are perpendicular.
A drawing that looks at right angles can be out of scale. Find the mark or the given fact.

examples.title: A missing angle
examples.question:
Three of four sectors around a point are 63°, 65° and 80°.

  1. Find the fourth angle.

    [2]

  2. Explain where the total of 360° comes from.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The three angles add to 208°.

Take this from 360°.

\(152\) degrees.

(b) The sectors fill the turn without gaps or overlap.

A complete turn is 360°.

examples.title: A missing angle
examples.question:
Three of the four interior angles of a quadrilateral are 76°, 65° and 78°.

  1. Find the fourth angle.

    [2]

  2. Explain where the total of 360° comes from.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The three angles add to 219°.

Take this from 360°.

\(141\) degrees.

(b) The two triangle angle sums add together at the original corners.

A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles. Each has angle sum 180°.

examples.title: A transversal across parallel paths
examples.question:
Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by a third straight line. At the top crossing, the angle above the horizontal line on the right of the transversal is 56°.

  1. Find the angle above the lower horizontal line on the right of the transversal.

    [2]

  2. Find the other angle above the lower horizontal line, to the left of the transversal.

    [2]

  3. At the bottom crossing, explain why the angle below the line on the left of the transversal has the same size as the first angle.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The two angles are in matching positions at their crossings.

They are corresponding angles, so they are equal.

\(56\) degrees.

(b) The two angles together make a straight line.

Subtract 56° from 180°.

\(124\) degrees.

(c) Both angles are equal to 180° minus the same neighbouring angle.

They are vertically opposite, so both are 56°.

examples.title: Splitting a right angle
examples.question:
Two lines meet at a right angle. A third line through the meeting point splits this right angle into 55° and x°.

  1. Find x.

    [2]

  2. Find the opposite angle of a° in this diagram if the lines are extended. Name the fact you use.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.

Subtract 55 from 90.

\(35\) degrees.

(b) Extending a straight line does not change the size of its existing angle.

It is 55°. Angles opposite each other at an intersection are equal.

  1. Find the angle above the lower horizontal line on the right of the transversal.

    [2]

  2. Find the other angle above the lower horizontal line, to the left of the transversal.

    [2]

  3. At the bottom crossing, explain why the angle below the line on the left of the transversal has the same size as the first angle.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(82\) degrees.

(b) \(98\) degrees.

(c) They are vertically opposite, so both are 82°.
questions.solution_html:
(a) The two angles are in matching positions at their crossings.

They are corresponding angles, so they are equal.

\(82\) degrees.

(b) The two angles together make a straight line.

Subtract 82° from 180°.

\(98\) degrees.

(c) Both angles are equal to 180° minus the same neighbouring angle.

They are vertically opposite, so both are 82°.
questions.hint_html: Match the positions to find corresponding angles.

questions.prompt_html:
Two lines meet at a right angle. A third line through the meeting point splits this right angle into 36° and x°.

  1. Find x.

    [2]

  2. Find the opposite angle of a° in this diagram if the lines are extended. Name the fact you use.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(54\) degrees.

(b) It is 36°. Angles opposite each other at an intersection are equal.
questions.solution_html:
(a) Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.

Subtract 36 from 90.

\(54\) degrees.

(b) Extending a straight line does not change the size of its existing angle.

It is 36°. Angles opposite each other at an intersection are equal.
